title: One Number for Many
question: How can one number stand for a whole pile of data?
hook: A shooting percentage squeezes a season of shots into a single figure.
idea: Descriptive statistics squeeze a sample into a few summary numbers or graphs that show its typical value and its spread.

beats.prompt: A player shoots 33%. Out of 30 shots, roughly how many went in?

choices.label: About 3
choices.feedback: This reads 33% as 3.3%, but 33% is about one in every three.

choices.label: About 20
choices.feedback: That would be two in every three, which is around 67%.

choices.label: About 33
choices.feedback: It copies the percentage as a count, but 33 would be more than 30 shots.

beats.explain: A player who shoots 33% is making approximately one shot in every three, so about 10 of 30.

beats.prompt: Sort each measure into the kind of property it describes.
beats.explain: Mean, median and mode are measures of central tendency; standard deviation and the minimum and maximum values are measures of variability.

beats.prompt: Match each summary to what it does.
pairs: Shots made divided by shots taken
One number for a student's general performance
A graph of a variable's distribution
A measure of dependence between two variables
beats.explain: Each one boils down many observations into a summary number or graph.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: A study draws its main conclusions with inferential statistics.
Its first table lists the overall sample size and subgroup sizes.
That table is a set of descriptive statistics.
So descriptive statistics never appear alongside inferential ones.
beats.explain: Even when a data analysis draws its main conclusions using inferential statistics, descriptive statistics are generally also presented.
